claim: 119 predicted protein-coding genes from intergenic regions occur only in the mouse genome, but not in rats or humans.
source: We were able to identify 119 predicted protein-coding genes from intergenic regions that occur only in the mouse genome, but not in rats or humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylostratigraphy and synteny-based analysis described in the methods section.

claim: 110 out of 119 candidate de novo genes have direct evidence for translation.
source: We found for 110 out of the 119 candidate genes direct evidence for translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling and peptide mass spectrometry datasets analysis.

claim: Testis and brain express the relatively largest abundance of candidate de novo genes.
source: Testis and brain express the relatively largest abundance of these candidate de novo genes, while the digestive system and liver express the lowest (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ENCODE RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: De novo genes have lower expression levels than other protein-coding genes.
source: Expression levels of these genes are generally lower than those of other protein-coding genes (FPKM medians: 0.63 vs. 8.18; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<2.2 × 10−16; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of FPKM values between de novo and other protein-coding genes.

claim: De novo genes have fewer exons than other protein-coding genes.
source: They have fewer exons (medians: 2 vs. 7; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<2.2 × 10−16)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of exon numbers.

claim: De novo genes have fewer coding exons than other protein-coding genes.
source: and fewer coding exons than other protein-coding genes (medians: 1 vs. 6; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of coding exon numbers.

claim: De novo gene proteins are shorter than other proteins.
source: The lengths of their proteins are shorter than those of other proteins (medians: 125 vs. 397; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of protein lengths.

claim: De novo gene proteins are predicted to be less disordered than other proteins.
source: However, their proteins are predicted to be less disordered than other proteins (medians: 0.20 vs. 0.27; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value=0.0024; Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by intrinsic structural disorder score predictions and statistical comparison.

claim: De novo gene proteins are equally hydrophobic to other proteins.
source: and equally hydrophobic to other proteins (medians: 0.56 vs. 0.57; two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value=0.52; Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by hydrophobic cluster analysis and statistical comparison.

claim: Gm13030 is only expressed in the ovary and subcutaneous adipose tissue according to ENCODE RNA-Seq data.
source: According to the ENCODE RNA-Seq data, Gm13030 is only expressed in two tissues, the ovary of 8 weeks old females (FPKM 0.135), as well as the subcutaneous adipose tissue of 8 weeks old animals (FPKM 0.115) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ENCODE RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Gm13030 is not expressed in the ovary, but predominantly in the oviduct.
source: We found that Gm13030 is not expressed in the ovary, but predominantly in the oviduct with only a weak signal from the adjacent fat pad (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reverse transcription PCR experiments on carefully prepared tissue samples.

claim: The Gm13030 ORF emerged between 2-4 million years ago.
source: But since both enabler mutations are at least seen in M. spicilegus, we place the emergence of the Gm13030 ORF at this node, that is between 2–4 million years ago.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of enabler mutations across mouse species.

claim: All three M. m. domesticus populations carry a 17nt deletion that leads to a disruption of the Gm13030 reading frame.
source: Most notably, all three M. m. domesticus populations carry a 17nt deletion that leads to a disruption of the reading frame.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus populations have retained the Gm13030 ORF after its emergence.
source: Hence, after the emergence of the Gm13030 ORF, only the M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus populations have retained it.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of secondary disablers across mouse populations.

claim: There is no traceable signal of positive selection on the Gm13030 protein after the emergence of the ORF.
source: Hence, we conclude that there is no traceable signal of positive selection on the protein after the emergence of the ORF.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of coding vs. non-coding substitution ratios shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 treatment introduced a 7 bp deletion at the beginning of the Gm13030 ORF causing a frameshift and premature stop codon.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 treatment introduced a 7 bp deletion at the beginning of the ORF (position 41–47) causing a frameshift and a premature stop codon in exon 2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing verification of the deletion.

claim: No off-target variants were found in the 100 bp regions around the 343 predicted off-target sites in the genome sequencing of the founding pair.
source: However, in our genome sequencing results, we found no variant located in the 100 bp regions around the genome-wide 343 predicted off-target sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing analysis of the founding pair.

claim: The Gm13030 knockout line is homozygous viable and fertile.
source: The Gm13030 knockout line is homozygous viable and fertile.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of the knockout line.

claim: No differentially expressed genes were found between knockouts and wildtypes in the initial analysis involving all oviduct samples.
source: In the initial analysis involving all samples, we found no differentially expressed gene between knockouts and wildtypes.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq differential expression analysis.

claim: The oviduct transcriptomes cluster into three major groups corresponding to different phases of the estrous cycle.
source: Given that the expression in oviducts should be fluctuating according to estrous cycle, we clustered the transcriptomes of the individuals based on both principle component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical clustering methods, which allowed to distinguish three major clusters (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA and hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: 21 genes are differentially expressed in cluster 1 between knockout and wildtype samples.
source: We found 21 differentially expressed genes in cluster 1 (DESeq2, adjusted p-value≤0.01; fold changes range from 0.75 to 1.59; Table 1), but still none for clusters 2 and 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis on cluster 1 samples.

claim: Gm13030 acts during the phase of high progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor 1 expression, and low G protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1 expression.
source: This suggests that Gm13030 acts during the phase of high progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor 1 expression, and low G protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1 expression, corresponding to proestrus or the starting of estrus, that is, the phase where females start to become receptive for implantation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression patterns of sex hormone receptor genes in cluster 1 shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Dcpp1, Dcpp2, and Dcpp3 are significantly upregulated in knockout samples in cluster 1.
source: The top three differentially expressed genes belong all to a single young gene family, namely Dcpp1, Dcpp2 and Dcpp3, all three of which were significantly up-regulated in the knockout samples (DESeq2, fold changes: 1.45 for Dcpp1, 1.47 for Dcpp2, and 1.59 for Dcpp3, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis and confirmed by quantitative PCR assay.

claim: Dcpp genes are expressed in female and male reproductive organs and the thymus.
source: These genes are expressed in female and male reproductive organs and the thymus, and were previously found to function in oviducts to stimulate pre-implantation embryo development (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Dcpp genes function in oviducts to stimulate pre-implantation embryo development.
source: These genes are expressed in female and male reproductive organs and the thymus, and were previously found to function in oviducts to stimulate pre-implantation embryo development (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Rxfp1 is the receptor for the pregnancy hormone relaxin.
source: The fourth gene in the list of significantly changed expression is Rxfp1, the receptor for the pregnancy hormone relaxin.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Rxfp1.

claim: Relaxin signaling is involved in regulation of the reproductive cycle.
source: Relaxin signaling is involved in a variety of cellular processes (Valkovic et al., 2019), whereby the regulation of the reproductive cycle is one of them (Anand-Ivell and Ivell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Valkovic et al., 2019 and Anand-Ivell and Ivell, 2014.

claim: Homozygous knockout females produce their second litter faster than wildtype or heterozygous females.
source: However, we saw a major difference with respect to the second litter. Homozygous knockout females tended to produce this faster than wildtype or heterozygous females (medians: 23 vs. 38 days, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data from normal breeding stocks and confirmed by additional mating pairs.

claim: The difference in time to second litter between knockout and wildtype/heterozygous females is statistically significant.
source: When using the two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test which does not require the assumption of a normal distribution, we found that this difference is significant when calculated across all breeding data (p-value=0.042).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of breeding data.

claim: About a quarter of litters from homozygous knockout females show infanticide, but none from wildtype or heterozygous females.
source: Interestingly, we found not only a timing difference for the second litter but also infanticide in about a quarter of the litters (4 out of 16) from homozygous females, but none in wildtype or heterozygous females (two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p-value=0.031, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding observations and statistical analysis.

claim: Homozygous knockout females have similar litter sizes to wildtype or heterozygous females.
source: In addition, one could also have expected to see homozygous knockout females having larger litter sizes than those of wildtype or heterozygous females, but they were almost the same (medians: 6.5 vs. 7.0 for littler 1 and 6.5 vs. 7.5 for litter 2, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data.

claim: Dcpp3 was lost in M. m. domesticus populations.
source: Intriguingly, when inspecting the copy number variation data that we have produced previously (Pezer et al., 2015), we found that Dcpp3 was also lost in M. m. domesticus populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by copy number variation data from Pezer et al., 2015.

claim: The loss of Gm13030 should be detrimental to animals in the wild.
source: These results suggest that the loss of Gm13030 should be detrimental to the animals in the wild.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed phenotypes of shorter intervals to second birth and higher infanticide rates.

claim: The secondary loss of Dcpp3 in M. m. domesticus could compensate for the loss of Gm13030.
source: Under the assumption that this results in an overall lowered expression of Dcpp RNAs, it could be considered to compensate for the loss of Gm13030.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that both Gm13030 and Dcpp3 are lost in M. m. domesticus.

claim: The knockout has an impact on the transcriptome in the oviduct only at a specific stage of the female estrous cycle.
source: We find that the knockout has an impact on the transcriptome in the oviduct only at a specific stage of the female estrous cycle, and we also find a unique female-specific phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis showing differential expression only in cluster 1.

claim: Gm13030 is named Shiji (Shj) after a female figure born from stone in Chinese mythology.
source: Hence, we propose to give a formal name to Gm13030. We name it after a female figure, Shiji (Shj), who was born from stone (de novo) as a mythology character in the Chinese traditional novel Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), which was published in the 16th century.
evidence: The claim is a naming decision by the authors based on the de novo origin of the gene.

claim: Dcpp expression is induced in the oviduct by pre-implantation embryos and is then secreted into the oviduct.
source: Dcpp expression is induced in the oviduct by pre-implantation embryos and is then secreted into the oviduct. This in turn stimulates the further maturation of the embryos and eventually the implantation (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Shj could have found its function in controlling Dcpp expression, defending the interests of the mother.
source: Hence, this is a system where a selfish tendency for Dcpp expression favoring embryo implantation could develop, in expense of the interest of the mother that wants to build up new resources first. Accordingly, Shj could have found its function in controlling this expression, that is, 'defending' the interests of the mother.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed upregulation of Dcpp genes in knockouts and the phenotypic consequences.

claim: An evolutionary conflict of interest exists for the interactions between Shj and Dcpp genes.
source: This is compatible with the notion that an evolutionary conflict of interest exists for these interactions, whereby it remains open whether the loss of Dcpp3 preceded the loss of Shj or vice versa.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-occurrence of Shj and Dcpp3 losses in M. m. domesticus.

claim: Shj inactivation alleles segregate in M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus populations in low frequency.
source: We note that Shj inactivation alleles segregate also in the populations of the other subspecies (M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus) in low frequency, implying that the evolutionary process of fully integrating this new gene is still ongoing.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There has been much focus on de novo genes to have male-biased expression and to affect male fertility.
source: There has so far been much focus on de novo genes and other new genes to have male-biased expression and to affect male fertility (Chen et al., 2013; Ellegren and Parsch, 2007; Heinen et al., 2009; Kaessmann, 2010; Long et al., 2013; Reinhardt et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Arts, a duplicated gene in Drosophila, has high expression in the ovary and affects fertility.
source: Only recently, one of a pair of duplicated genes in Drosophila, Arts, has been shown to have high expression in the ovary and to affect fertility (VanKuren and Long, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to VanKuren and Long, 2018.

claim: Female reproduction should be subject to accelerated evolution patterns, especially in mammals.
source: Female reproduction should be subject to accelerated evolution patterns, especially in mammals which have high complexities in female reproduction, including mate choice, pregnancy, and parenting, which has been neglected so far.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the complexity of female reproduction in mammals.

claim: The estrous cycle in females adds to the complexity of analyzing biased gene expression.
source: One reason is that the estrous cycle in females adds to the complexity of the analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experience with the current study.

claim: The large number of new genes transcribed in testis is due to the promiscuous phase of expression in meiotic cells.
source: Another reason for the current focus on males is the large number of new genes that are transcribed in testis. However, this is due to the promiscuous phase of expression in meiotic cells, where many genes use alternative promotors (Kleene, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kleene, 2001.

claim: Meiotic cells are abundant in testis but difficult to analyze in ovaries.
source: These meiotic cells are abundant in testis, but are difficult to analyze in ovaries.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the differences in meiotic cell abundance between testis and ovaries.

claim: Shj exerts its effects in somatic cells, independent of possible expression in meiosis.
source: Shj exerts its effects in somatic cells, that is, independent of a possible expression in meiosis, but in the context of a possible selfish gene conflict situation, which has so far been ascribed mostly to the male reproductive system (Kleene, 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that Shj is expressed in the oviduct, a somatic tissue.

claim: It has long been assumed that the emergence of function out of non-coding DNA regions must be rare.
source: It has long been assumed that the emergence of function out of non-coding DNA regions must be rare, and if it occurs, the resulting genes would be far away from assuming a function.
evidence: The claim refers to historical assumptions in the field.

claim: The results do not support the assumption that de novo gene emergence is rare or that resulting genes are far from assuming a function.
source: Our results do not support these assumptions.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of the current study showing functional effects of Shj.

claim: It is possible to find many well supported transcripts that could be considered to be true de novo genes.
source: It is possible to find many well supported transcripts that could be considered to be true de novo genes.
evidence: The claim is based on the identification of 119 candidate de novo genes with translation evidence.

claim: Shj has functions on the transcriptome and the phenotype.
source: We have shown here that Shj has functions on the transcriptome and the phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and breeding experiments.

claim: The Shj ORF has acquired only a small number of additional substitutions after it emerged.
source: The Shj ORF has acquired only a small number of additional substitutions, both coding and non-coding after it emerged.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Shj did not need additional adaptation of the protein sequence to become functional.
source: This suggests that it did not need additional adaptation of the protein sequence to become functional.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of positive selection signal and the small number of substitutions.

claim: A similar analysis on a larger set of de novo ORFs in the mouse shows lack of additional adaptation.
source: This is in line with a similar analysis on a larger set of de novo ORFs in the mouse (Ruiz-Orera et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ruiz-Orera et al., 2018.

claim: Signatures of positive selection around de novo genes should not necessarily be expected as proof that it is a true gene.
source: Hence, this raises the question whether we should necessarily expect signatures of positive selection around de novo genes as part of proof that it is a true gene (McLysaght and Hurst, 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative, questioning a common assumption in the field.

claim: A large set of expressed random sequences can exert phenotypes.
source: Alternatively, given the observation that a large set of expressed random sequences can exert phenotypes (Bao et al., 2017; Neme et al., 2017), it would seem more likely that the conversion of a non-coding region into a coding one would already be sufficient to create a gene function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2017 and Neme et al., 2017.

claim: In the early phase of evolution, de novo genes would likely be frequently subject to secondary loss.
source: In the early phase of evolution, such genes would likely be frequently subject to secondary loss (Palmieri et al., 2014), but they could eventually also become fixed and then further evolutionarily optimized.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Palmieri et al., 2014 and is consistent with the observation of secondary losses in the current study.

claim: The conversion of a non-coding region into a coding one would already be sufficient to create a gene function.
source: Alternatively, given the observation that a large set of expressed random sequences can exert phenotypes (Bao et al., 2017; Neme et al., 2017), it would seem more likely that the conversion of a non-coding region into a coding one would already be sufficient to create a gene function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on cited evidence about random sequences and the findings of the current study.

claim: A de novo evolved gene can directly adopt a function without much sequence adaptation.
source: Given that Gm13030 shows no signs of positive selection, our findings support the hypothesis that a de novo evolved gene can directly adopt a function without much sequence adaptation.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of positive selection signal and the observed functional effects of Shj.

claim: The interruption of the Gm13030 reading frame affects the transcriptional network in the oviducts at a specific stage of the estrous cycle.
source: The interruption of the reading frame affects the transcriptional network in the oviducts at a specific stage of the estrous cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis showing differential expression only in cluster 1.

claim: The interruption of Gm13030 includes the upregulation of Dcpp genes.
source: This includes the upregulation of Dcpp genes, which are known to stimulate the growth of preimplantation embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq and ddPCR analysis.

claim: Dcpp genes are known to stimulate the growth of preimplantation embryos.
source: This includes the upregulation of Dcpp genes, which are known to stimulate the growth of preimplantation embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge, likely from Lee et al., 2006 cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Knockout females have their second litters after shorter times.
source: As a consequence, knockout females have their second litters after shorter times and have a higher infanticide rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data.

claim: Knockout females have a higher infanticide rate.
source: As a consequence, knockout females have their second litters after shorter times and have a higher infanticide rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding observations.

claim: The de novo emergence of new genes has been well documented through genomic analyses.
source: The de novo emergence of new genes has been well documented through genomic analyses.
evidence: The claim refers to established knowledge in the field.

claim: Functional analysis of very young protein-coding genes is still largely lacking.
source: However, a functional analysis, especially of very young protein-coding genes, is still largely lacking.
evidence: The claim refers to a gap in the current state of research.

claim: The evolution of new genes through duplication-divergence processes is well understood.
source: The evolution of new genes through duplication-divergence processes is well understood (Chen et al., 2013; Kaessmann, 2010; Long et al., 2013; Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The evolution of new genes from non-coding DNA has been little considered for a long time.
source: But the evolution of new genes from non-coding DNA has been little considered for a long time (Tautz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tautz, 2014.

claim: With increasing availability of comparative genome data, more cases of de novo gene emergence have been described.
source: However, with the increasing availability of comparative genome data from closely related species, more and more cases of unequivocal de novo gene emergence have been described (McLysaght and Hurst, 2016; Schlötterer, 2015; Tautz, 2014; Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: De novo gene emergence is a very active process in all evolutionary lineages analyzed.
source: These analyses have shown that de novo gene emergence is a very active process in all evolutionary lineages analyzed.
evidence: The claim is based on cited comparative genomic analyses.

claim: Virtually the whole genome is 'scanned' by transcript emergence and loss within about 10 million years of mouse evolutionary history.
source: A comparative analysis of closely related mouse species has even suggested that virtually the whole genome is 'scanned' by transcript emergence and loss within about 10 million years of evolutionary history (Neme and Tautz, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Neme and Tautz, 2016.

claim: Functional studies of de novo genes have lacked behind the detection of their transcriptional and translational expression.
source: But unlike the detection of the transcriptional and translational expression of de novo genes, functional studies of such genes have lacked behind.
evidence: The claim refers to a gap in the current state of research.

claim: In yeast, the de novo evolved gene BSC4 was found to be involved in DNA repair.
source: In yeast, the de novo evolved gene BSC4 was found to be involved in DNA repair (Cai et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2008.

claim: In yeast, MDF1 was found to suppress mating and to promote fermentation.
source: and MDF1 (Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014) was found to suppress mating and to promote fermentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: Knockdown of candidates of de novo genes in Drosophila have suggested effects on viability and male fertility.
source: Knockdown of candidates of de novo genes in Drosophila have suggested effects on viability and male fertility (Chen et al., 2010; Reinhardt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010 and Reinhardt et al., 2013.

claim: Male fertility was found to be affected for Pldi in mice, which codes for a lncRNA.
source: Male fertility was also found to be affected for Pldi in mice, which codes for a lncRNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge, likely from Heinen et al., 2009 cited elsewhere.

claim: The knockout of Pldi was shown to affect sperm motility and testis weight.
source: In this case the knockout was shown to affect sperm motility and testis weight (Heinen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heinen et al., 2009.

claim: Mammalian females have complex reproduction cycles, including morphology, physiology and behavior relating to mate choice, pregnancy, and parenting.
source: However, considering that the mammalian females have complex reproduction cycles, including morphology, physiology and behavior relating to mate choice, pregnancy, and parenting, de novo genes in mammals should also be expected to have a function in female-specific organs and affect female fertility and reproductive behavior as well.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mammalian female reproduction.

claim: De novo genes in mammals should be expected to have a function in female-specific organs and affect female fertility and reproductive behavior.
source: However, considering that the mammalian females have complex reproduction cycles, including morphology, physiology and behavior relating to mate choice, pregnancy, and parenting, de novo genes in mammals should also be expected to have a function in female-specific organs and affect female fertility and reproductive behavior as well.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the complexity of female reproduction.

claim: Most de novo genes are translated based on ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry data.
source: We have analyzed ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry data for these and find that most of them are translated.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The emergence of Gm13030 may have been driven by an evolutionary conflict situation.
source: We conclude that it functions in the oviduct and affects female fertility cycles and that its emergence may have been driven by an evolutionary conflict situation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed interactions between Shj and Dcpp genes.

claim: Random protein sequences have a good probability for conveying evolutionarily relevant functions.
source: These results support the notion that random protein sequences have a good probability for conveying evolutionarily relevant functions (Neme et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Neme et al., 2017 and the findings of the current study.

claim: The Gm13030 allele in C57BL/6N represents the non-interrupted version found in M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus.
source: and the Gm13030 allele represents indeed the non-interrupted version that is found in M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison with the reference genome and wild populations.

claim: The 21 differentially expressed genes in cluster 1 do not include the genes neighboring Gm13030.
source: The 21 differentially expressed genes in cluster 1 do not include the genes neighboring Gm13030 (Pla2g2e and Pla2g5).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq differential expression analysis.

claim: When the second litter follows too quickly, females may be under stronger postpartum stress resulting in partial killing of pups.
source: This could indicate that when the second litter follows too quickly, the females may be under stronger postpartum stress resulting in partial killing of pups.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed correlation between shorter intervals and infanticide.

claim: More pups from homozygous knockout females may have been eaten before being observed, explaining similar litter sizes.
source: One possible explanation is that considering the high infanticide rate for homozygous knockouts, more pups from homozygous knockout females were eaten before being observed.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offered as a possible explanation for the lack of difference in litter sizes.

claim: Females can ovulate within a day of giving birth.
source: Females can ovulate within a day of giving birth, but if no successful mating occurs at that time, ovulation is suppressed while the female is lactating.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse reproductive biology.

claim: Ovulation is suppressed while the female is lactating if no successful mating occurs shortly after giving birth.
source: Females can ovulate within a day of giving birth, but if no successful mating occurs at that time, ovulation is suppressed while the female is lactating.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse reproductive biology.

claim: Suppression of ovulation during lactation results in a delay in the timing of the next pregnancy.
source: This results in a delay in the timing of the next pregnancy.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse reproductive biology.

claim: The bimodal distribution pattern of time to second litter is evident in the data.
source: Figure 5 shows that this pattern is also evident in our data.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Times to the second litter were either smaller than or equal to 25 days (early group) or larger than or equal to 35 days (late group).
source: We found that the times to the second litter were either smaller than or equal to 25 days (early group) or larger than or equal to 35 days (late group) for both the homozygous knockout females and the wildtype or heterozygous females.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of breeding data.

claim: In homozygous knockouts, more females were in the early group for second litter timing.
source: But in the homozygous knockouts, we saw more in the early group, leading to the median values having a big difference.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of breeding data.
